atlas_home_region_card.compact: A downtown New York scene/ecosystem where punk urgency, art-school experiment, poetry, pop instincts, minimal electronics, and club culture collided around CBGB and nearby venues rather than resolving into one sound.
atlas_home_region_card.standard: This scene changed what a rock band could be after the 1960s. It helped punk and new wave separate from classic-rock scale, proved that small rooms and original songs could generate durable lineages, and opened roads into post-punk, college rock, indie, noise rock, synth-punk, art-pop, and modern downtown/retro-shadow guitar music. Historically important does not automatically mean user-specific fit: Atlas should treat each branch as a separate test.

mission_detail_history_module.compact: What this route tests: A downtown New York scene/ecosystem where punk urgency, art-school experiment, poetry, pop instincts, minimal electronics, and club culture collided around CBGB and nearby venues rather than resolving into one sound.
mission_detail_history_module.standard: CBGB opened in 1973 on the Bowery under Hilly Kristal and became a practical home for original underground rock. What later looks like “the CBGB sound” was actually a cluster of incompatible but mutually intensifying bands: Patti Smith fused rock and poetry; Television stretched guitar interplay into nervous art-rock; Talking Heads turned anxiety, rhythm, and conceptual framing into new wave; Blondie smuggled girl-group/pop/disco instincts through downtown cool; Richard Hell gave punk a persona of damaged refusal; Suicide reduced rock to voice, synth pulse, and menace; and No Wave pushed the scene toward abrasive boundary testing. It helps place this road in a broader music-history context.
mission_detail_history_module.deep: CBGB opened in 1973 on the Bowery under Hilly Kristal and became a practical home for original underground rock. What later looks like “the CBGB sound” was actually a cluster of incompatible but mutually intensifying bands: Patti Smith fused rock and poetry; Television stretched guitar interplay into nervous art-rock; Talking Heads turned anxiety, rhythm, and conceptual framing into new wave; Blondie smuggled girl-group/pop/disco instincts through downtown cool; Richard Hell gave punk a persona of damaged refusal; Suicide reduced rock to voice, synth pulse, and menace; and No Wave pushed the scene toward abrasive boundary testing. This scene changed what a rock band could be after the 1960s. It helped punk and new wave separate from classic-rock scale, proved that small rooms and original songs could generate durable lineages, and opened roads into post-punk, college rock, indie, noise rock, synth-punk, art-pop, and modern downtown/retro-shadow guitar music. Historically important does not automatically mean user-specific fit: Atlas should treat each branch as a separate test.

did_you_know_card.compact: The initials came from “Country, Bluegrass, Blues,” but the club became famous because it gave original underground rock bands a room, a stage, and a scene.
did_you_know_card.standard: CBGB mattered because it gave incompatible original bands the same room. Patti Smith, Television, Blondie, Suicide, and James Chance prove this was a scene, not one sound.
did_you_know_card.deep: CBGB mattered because it gave incompatible original bands the same room. Patti Smith, Television, Blondie, Suicide, and James Chance prove this was a scene, not one sound.
